title: The US Said Green Card Applicants Must Leave the Country. A Week Later, It Said Never Mind.
excerpt: A USCIS memo on adjustment of status has triggered panic among Indian H-1B holders. DHS walked it back within days, but immigration lawyers say the damage is already done.
body:
For ten days, hundreds of thousands of Indian immigrants in the United States lived with a question that no one in Washington seemed able to answer clearly: would they have to leave the country to get a green card?

On May 21, US Citizenship and Immigration Services issued a policy memorandum — PM-602-0199 — that appeared to overturn decades of settled practice. The memo declared that adjustment of status, the process by which immigrants already living in the US apply for permanent residency without leaving, should henceforth be treated as "extraordinary discretionary relief" rather than the routine pathway it has been for decades.

The language was stark. A USCIS spokesman said that "from now on, an alien who is in the US temporarily and wants a green card must return to their home country to apply, except in extraordinary circumstances."

By May 30, the Department of Homeland Security was scrambling to walk it back.

## What Changed — and What DHS Now Says

The original memo sent shockwaves through immigrant communities, employers, and immigration law firms across the country. Approximately 820,000 people apply for green cards through adjustment of status each year. In 2024 alone, roughly 1.4 million green cards were issued, a significant share of them through this in-country process.

The adjustment of status route has been especially critical for Indian nationals on H-1B and L-1 visas, who often wait years — sometimes over a decade — for their priority dates to become current due to per-country caps on employment-based green cards. During that wait, they build lives, buy homes, raise children, and contribute to their communities. Being told to leave the country mid-process would upend everything.

After a week of mounting alarm, a DHS spokesperson told the New York Times that "this move was just a reminder to officers of their discretionary authority, which has always existed on a case-by-case basis." A senior White House official described it as a "routine administrative step" rather than a major policy change.

But immigration lawyers are not reassured.

## Lawyers Say the Chaos Is the Point

CNN spoke with half a dozen immigration attorneys who uniformly described the situation as deliberately ambiguous. "They want it to be arbitrary and capricious," said immigration attorney Jim Hacking. "They want people to be scared, and they want people to leave the US voluntarily."

Charles Kuck, an Atlanta-based immigration attorney, offered a more measured view but was equally blunt. "I bet you there's a million pending adjustment applications, easy. You cannot say now to those million people, 'Thanks for your money, I need you to go to your home country and restart this all over again.' No judge upholds that — none."

Kuck emphasized that adjustment of status is not a loophole. "When Congress amends and betters a law 20 times, it's hard to call that a loophole," he said. "It is the law, and the law will continue to allow for adjustment of status for individuals who otherwise qualify inside the United States."

Maureen Sweeney, a University of Maryland law professor, called the move part of a broader pattern. "I think this is yet another very clear indication that this is a nationalist campaign, not just a campaign to clean up the immigration service," she said. "I don't think this administration was ever interested in a functional immigration system."

## USCIS Is Already Applying the New Framework

Despite the walkback, evidence suggests that USCIS adjudicators are already incorporating the memo's guidance. CNN obtained a request for evidence on a pending adjustment of status case that asks applicants to demonstrate whether one of a dozen factors might weigh in their favor — including hardship to family members if denied, evidence of community service, and fluency in English.

These criteria did not previously exist as standard considerations for routine adjustment of status applications. Their introduction signals that even if mass denials are unlikely, the bar for approval has quietly risen.

## What This Means for Indian Immigrants

Indians are disproportionately affected by this policy shift for several reasons. They constitute the largest single nationality group among H-1B visa holders. They face the longest green card backlogs, with some employment-based categories showing wait times of over 50 years. And because of those backlogs, hundreds of thousands of Indian professionals have been living in the US on temporary work visas for years or decades while their green card applications inch forward.

The memo comes just weeks after USCIS confirmed that EB-2 green card slots for Indian nationals are exhausted for fiscal year 2026, with no new approvals possible until October. Together, these developments paint a picture of an immigration system that is increasingly hostile to the very skilled workers it was designed to attract.

For NRIs with pending applications, immigration lawyers are counseling patience. The policy change is administrative, not legislative, and is almost certain to face legal challenges. But the anxiety is real, the uncertainty is corrosive, and the message — whether intended or not — is being heard clearly by a generation of Indian professionals deciding where to build their futures.

"We have options, and we're fighting really hard to stay in the US and contribute economically," one green card applicant, a PhD researcher married to an American citizen, told CNN. "But if that's not a possibility, we are competitive in other markets, and we'll have no other choice but to take our family elsewhere."

That brain drain is no longer theoretical. It is happening in real time.
author: Diaspora Desk
